segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll, written on the inside and on the back, sealed up with seven seals.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw a strong angel proclaiming in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one in heaven or on the earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I wept bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of the elders said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not weep. Look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw, in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though slaughtered, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he came and took it from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a lyre and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they sang a new song, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you bought people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you made them a kingdom and priests for our God, and they reign on the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slaughtered to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And every creature in heaven and on the earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the four living creatures said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Amen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the elders fell down and worshiped.

notes.phrase: written on the inside and on the back
notes.traditional: a book written within and on the backside
notes.note: The word denotes a papyrus or parchment roll, not a bound book. Scrolls were normally written on the inner side only, so one written on both sides is unusually full; the image recalls the scroll shown to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Legal documents such as wills and deeds were closed with multiple seals, which had to be broken before the contents could be read or put into effect. The Greek says literally 'upon the right hand', so the scroll may be pictured as lying on the open palm.

notes.phrase: the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
notes.traditional: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
notes.note: Both titles are drawn from Scripture and were read as pointing to the Messiah: Judah is called a lion in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9–10), and Isaiah 11:1, 10 speaks of a shoot from the root of Jesse, David's father. 'Root' here probably means a growth from the root, that is, a descendant of David's line, though some take it to mean David's source.

notes.phrase: in the midst of the throne
notes.traditional: in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders
notes.note: The Greek repeats 'in the midst of' in a way that can be read two ways. Either the Lamb stands at the centre, where the throne and living creatures are, surrounded by the elders, or the Lamb stands between the throne with its living creatures on one side and the elders on the other. The rendering keeps the Greek wording and leaves both possibilities open.

The verb is the ordinary word for butchering an animal, used in the Septuagint for sacrificial slaughter and also for violent killing of people. 'Slain' has become a solemn, archaic word that loses this bluntness. Several modern versions also use 'slaughtered'. The same word recurs in verses 9 and 12.

In Jewish Scripture a horn is a standard image of strength and royal power, and seven signifies completeness. The eyes echo Zechariah 4:10, where seven lamps are 'the eyes of the Lord, which range through the whole earth'. Whether 'the seven spirits of God' refers to the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness or to seven angelic beings before the throne is disputed.

The kithara was a lyre: a handheld instrument with strings stretched from a sound box to a crossbar, and the usual Septuagint word for the instrument of the temple musicians. Most English versions say 'harp', which suggests a different and larger instrument. Some recent translations use 'lyre'.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense here. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

notes.traditional: redeemed (KJV); ransomed or purchased in many modern versions
notes.note: This is the everyday marketplace word for buying, and it was also used of purchasing slaves. 'Redeemed' and 'ransomed' translate it with words that in English belong to other Greek terms and carry more theological freight than this verb does by itself. The price is named in the same clause: 'with your blood'.

The Greek text translated here has no stated object for 'bought'; 'people' is supplied because English requires one. Many later manuscripts add 'us', and correspondingly read 'made us' and 'we shall reign' in verse 10, which is the basis of the King James wording. Most modern editions judge the shorter reading original, with 'them' in verse 10.

The same Greek word is translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament where its plural refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here, in a fourfold list covering all humanity, it means a nation as an ethnic or political unit. The list echoes similar ones in Daniel (for example Daniel 7:14).

notes.traditional: we shall reign on the earth
notes.note: Manuscripts are divided between the present 'they reign' and the future 'they will reign'; the Greek text followed here reads the present, while many translations follow the future. The present may itself look ahead to what is certain. The preposition can also mean 'over the earth'. 'A kingdom and priests' echoes Exodus 19:6, where Israel is called a kingdom of priests.

notes.traditional: fell down and worshipped him that liveth for ever and ever
notes.note: Some late manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'the twenty-four elders' and add 'him who lives forever and ever' as the object of worship. The earliest witnesses lack both expansions, and modern editions omit them. Without the addition, the worship is directed to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, who are named together in verse 13.

candidates.reason: A key verb in Revelation and the Johannine letters, rendered variously as 'conquer', 'overcome', 'triumph' or 'be victorious'; the verbal thread is lost if the English varies.
Covers both physical prostration or homage before a superior and worship of a deity; the Gospels and Revelation need a consistent policy on when 'worship' is warranted.

candidates.rendering: forever and ever (for εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων)
candidates.reason: The 'ages of ages' formula and related phrases recur throughout the New Testament, and translators differ on whether to keep the Semitic idiom or render it 'forever'.
Rendered 'book' or 'scroll' in different places (the book of life, the scroll of Isaiah, the sealed scroll), and readers may not realise it is one word for one physical form.
Used of Jewish council members, church leaders, older men and the heavenly figures of Revelation; needs one decision on 'elder' versus alternatives across these senses.
